title: 45-Day Identification Strategy
name: 45-Day Identification Strategy
metaTitle: 45-Day Identification Strategy in Oklahoma City, OK
metaDescription: Building a defensible 45-day identification list for Oklahoma City replacement property, with real time built in for roof, dock, and HVAC checks.

sections.html: Forty-five days sounds like plenty of time until you try to fit a roof inspection, a dock door walkthrough, and a mechanical review into it for three different candidate buildings at once. Anyone who has scheduled facilities work on a deadline knows the calendar fills up faster than the task list suggests, and an exchange identification list built without accounting for that reality tends to fall apart in the final week rather than in the planning stage.

sections.heading: What the Window Actually Requires
sections.html: From the day the relinquished property sells, the investor has 45 calendar days to deliver a written identification of replacement candidates to the qualified intermediary, using either the three-property rule, the 200% rule, or the 95% rule as the counting method. There is no extension for a slow appraisal or a vendor who cannot get on site until next week. Whatever gets named on day 45 is what the rest of the exchange has to work with, which is why the identification decision deserves the same operational scrutiny an experienced facilities team would apply to any building it was about to take responsibility for, rather than a quick read of the listing sheet alone.

sections.heading: Building the List Around Real Inspection Time
sections.html: A distribution building near the I-40 and I-35 crossroads or a flex space closer to Tinker Air Force Base cannot be seriously identified without at least a walk of the loading docks, a look at roof age, and a rough read on the HVAC and warehouse lighting. That work has to be scheduled inside the 45 days, not after, which means the identification list is really being built backward from how much inspection time each candidate needs. A building with three dock doors and one rooftop unit clears faster than one with a dozen doors and a split system that needs a specialist to evaluate. Investors who treat every candidate as equally quick to vet, rather than sizing the inspection workload before committing time to it, are the ones who run out of window before the list is actually defensible.

sections.heading: Why Aerospace-Adjacent Space Moves on Its Own Clock
sections.html: Space serving aerospace supply chain tenants near Tinker often comes with specialized power, compressed air lines, or crane systems that a general inspector cannot fully evaluate on a single visit. If a candidate on the list falls into that category, the smart move is scheduling the specialist walkthrough in the first two weeks of the window, not the last few days, so a disqualifying finding still leaves time to name a backup property before day 45 closes.

sections.heading: Where Facilities Details Trip Up a List
sections.html:
• naming a candidate before confirming who has legal access to schedule a walkthrough
  • assuming a listing description of roof or HVAC condition without an actual inspection
  • underestimating how long a specialized aerospace-adjacent building takes to properly evaluate
  • forgetting to confirm dock door count and clear height match the intended use before identifying the property
  • waiting until the final week to schedule any inspection at all

sections.heading: Naming Backups Without Wasting the Window
sections.html: A second or third candidate on the identification list is only useful if there was enough time left to actually look at it. Investors who spend the first thirty days chasing one preferred building sometimes have no runway left to properly vet a backup if that first deal falls apart on inspection. Spreading walkthroughs across the full 45 days, rather than concentrating them at the end, keeps every named property equally defensible if the primary choice does not hold up. That means booking the second and third inspections in parallel with the first rather than waiting to see how the top choice turns out, even though it costs more inspection fees up front than doing them one at a time.

faqs.q: Does the 45-day identification window allow any extra time for building inspections?
faqs.a: No, the window runs on calendar days from the relinquished sale with no exception for inspection scheduling delays. Any roof, dock, or mechanical review needed to seriously evaluate a candidate has to happen inside that same window.

faqs.q: How is a warehouse near Tinker Air Force Base different to inspect than a standard flex building?
faqs.a: Aerospace-adjacent space sometimes includes specialized power, compressed air, or crane infrastructure that a general building inspector cannot fully assess, so a specialist visit may be needed. Scheduling that early in the window leaves room to pivot if the finding is unfavorable.

faqs.q: Can I identify a property I haven't physically walked yet?
faqs.a: You can name it on the list, but identifying a candidate without confirming its condition is a real risk since the window to swap it out for a better-vetted alternative is fixed and does not reopen after day 45.

faqs.q: What if my identification list falls apart after day 45?
faqs.a: Once the window closes, the list is locked, and any candidate not properly identified in writing to the qualified intermediary cannot be added. This is why spreading inspections across the full window matters more than rushing to name properties early.

faqs.q: Do I need a written identification even if I already know which property I want?
faqs.a: Yes. A verbal understanding or a signed letter of intent does not satisfy the requirement. The qualified intermediary needs a written, unambiguous description delivered before the 45th day regardless of how confident the investor is in the choice, and that description should be specific enough that a stranger reading it could locate the exact building without guessing.
